en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on King Udayana, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, where the king was named Udayana. Kauśāmbī...
In the country of Shen, there was a man named Ma-hui-ti who had a daughter of exquisite beauty, whose splendor was rarely matched in the world.
Seeing that his daughter’s countenance was so rare as to be unprecedented in the entire kingdom, her father named her Wu-bi (The Peerless).
The kings of neighboring states, their various officials, and the prominent clansmen all sought her hand in marriage;
her father replied,
"If there is a gentleman whose appearance matches that of my daughter, I shall accept his proposal."

At that time, as the Buddha was traveling through that country, Śreṇika beheld the Buddha’s thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs; his body was the color of purple-gold, majestic and sublime, with a radiance and deportment beyond compare. His heart filled with joy, he said:
"My daughter has found her match."
Returning home, he said to his wife,
"I have found a match for our daughter who is peerless.
He then hurriedly prepared his daughter with fine ornaments and set out to take her there.

The husband and wife dressed themselves together; their daughter, Bupoyaohua (Step-yao-hua), was resplendent with light, and she adorned herself with pearls and necklaces that illuminated the land. Together, the husband and wife led their daughter to where the Buddha was.
The wife saw the marks and signs upon the Buddha’s footprints, their radiant colors unlike anything found in the world; knowing him to be a World-Honored One, she said to her husband:

"The patterns of this man’s footprints are such as have never been heard of in the world; he must be extraordinary. He is surely pure and free from lust; he will certainly not take my daughter, so do not bring shame upon yourself."
The husband asked,
"How do you know this is so?
His wife then spoke these verses:
"The lustful man drags his heels as he walks; the angry man steps with his toes pointed;
the fool stumbles with his feet upon the ground; these are the tracks [of others], while this is the track of the Honored One among gods and humans."
Gosala said, "This is not something you women can understand; if you do not wish to do so, you may simply return home.
He then personally took his daughter to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Great Man has labored diligently in his instruction, yet his body receives no offerings.
There is this coarse woman; I pray that she may be provided with a winnowing basket and a broom.
The Buddha said:
"Do you consider this daughter to be beautiful?
He replied, "She was born with such exquisite features that she is truly peerless in the world; many kings and men of noble lineage have sought her hand, yet I did not grant their requests."
"I have observed that the Great Man’s radiance is majestic and far surpasses anything seen in this world; because I desire to obtain his offerings, I ought to take refuge in him.
The Buddha said, "In what respect is this woman's beauty so superior?"
Gosāla said, "From head to foot,
when I have observed him thoroughly, there is nothing about him that is not excellent.
The Buddha said:
"How deluded is the fleshly eye! As I observe it, from head to foot there is not a single thing that is good.
If there is hair upon the head, it is merely fur; the tails of elephants and horses are all the same.
Beneath the hair is the skull, which is merely bone; the skulls of pigs at the butcher's block are likewise so."

The brain within the head is like the putrid stench of mud; when it is brought down from the nose and placed upon the ground, no one can even step over it. The eyes are merely fragile vessels filled with pure fluids; the nose contains nasal mucus, and the mouth has only saliva. The internal organs—the liver and lungs—are likewise foul-smelling and rank. The intestines, stomach, and bladder consist only of excrement and urine, their putrid stench beyond description. The abdomen is a sack that wraps up all manner of impurities. The four limbs and hands and feet have bones supporting one another, tendons connecting them, and skin enveloping them; they move only by relying on the breath, like a wooden man operated by mechanical levers. Once this is finished, if one were to disassemble and lay out its body limb by limb, the hands and feet would lie in a chaotic mess.
Human beings are also like this; what excellence do they possess that you say they are "rarely matched"?

In the past, when I was beneath the Pāṭali tree, the sixth King of Māra adorned his three daughters with celestial beauty and splendor beyond compare in the heavens—not merely as such, but intending thereby to destroy my resolve for the Way. I spoke to them of the impurities within the body, and they were immediately transformed into the forms of old women, their beauty vanished and lost forever. Ashamed, they departed.
"Now that this is but a sack of excrement, what is there to be attached to?
Take it back at once; I will not accept it.
Having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, Śreṇika was suddenly overcome with shame and had no words left to say in reply. He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“If you, O Benevolent One, will not accept her, would it be acceptable to give her instead to King Udayana?
The Buddha did not answer.

Śāriputra then sent the woman to King Udayana. Upon receiving the woman, the king was greatly delighted; he appointed her father as Grand Tutor, built a palace for her, and provided a thousand musicians to attend upon her.
The king’s principal consort served as a teacher to the Buddha and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
This woman slandered her to the king, who, deluded by her words, shot his queen with a hundred arrows.

Later, seeing the arrows, the queen felt no fear and harbored no anger at all. With single-minded devotion to the Buddha and a heart of compassion, she knelt long before the king; the arrows then circled her three times and returned to stay in front of the king. This occurred in the same manner for all one hundred arrows.

The king was then startled and filled with trepidation; he immediately mounted a golden chariot drawn by white elephants and hastened to the Buddha’s dwelling. Before arriving, he alighted from his carriage and left his retinue behind, proceeding on foot to prostrate himself at the Buddha’s feet. Kneeling for a long time, he confessed: "I have committed grave offenses against the Triple Gem.

Because of those lewd and seductive women, I gave rise to lust and evil thoughts, harboring malevolent intentions toward the Buddha and the holy assembly. For every single evil thought, I shot a hundred arrows at the Buddha’s disciples. As I recount these matters, I am struck with fear at the sight of them. Yet even the compassionate power of a lay disciple, O Truly Enlightened One, is thus immeasurable; how much more so must that of the Unsurpassed, Truly Perfect Buddha be?"
"I now confess my transgressions and take refuge in the Triple Gem; may the Buddha’s vast compassion grant me forgiveness for my faults.
The Buddha smiled and said, "Excellent, O King!"
"To recognize one's evil and repent of one's transgressions—this is the conduct of a person of enlightenment; I accept the King’s kind intention.
The King bowed his head, repeating this three times, and the Buddha likewise accepted it three times.

The King again prostrated himself with his head to the ground, then withdrew to take his seat and said: "I have received a coarse and stubborn nature, prone to anger and self-indulgence, lacking any heart of forbearance.

The three poisons remain unremoved as I take pleasure in evil deeds; I follow the seductive and depraved ways of women without recognizing their wickedness. Reflecting on myself, I know that at the end of my life I will surely enter hell. I pray that the Buddha will show compassion and extensively explain the evil, demonic nature of women—how those caught in their snares rarely manage to extricate themselves. Having heard of these calamities, I shall surely use them as a warning to myself, so that the people, both great and small, may reform their conduct."
The Buddha said:
"What is the use of this question?
For now, let us discuss other matters."

The king said, "Other matters may be discussed on another day; it would not be too late. However, regarding the great calamity of a woman’s power to confuse and delude the mind—if one does not hear of its disaster, by what means can one distance oneself from it?"
"I pray that the Buddha will fully explain for me the transformations of the hells and the impurities of women.
The Buddha said,
"Listen attentively!"
"A man possesses the evil of lust, yet he beholds the female demon.
The King said, "Excellent!
I pray you accept my instruction."
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
There are four evils in men that you must urgently come to know."

In this world there are lustful men who constantly imagine seeing women and yearn to hear their seductive voices. They abandon the True Dharma from afar, harboring doubts about the truth while placing their faith in the false; ensnared by the net of lust, they sink into blinding darkness.

Driven by desire like a slave dreading his master, they crave the beauty of women and fail to perceive the foul stench of the impurities flowing from their nine apertures. Mired in the chaos of desire, they are like pigs in a sty who do not notice the stench but find it pleasant and take it as comfort, failing to consider that they shall later fall into the hells of the Unpleasant Pond to suffer endless pain.
With their minds fixed on lust, they consume their tears and spittle and revel in their pus and blood, treasuring them like jade and finding them as sweet as honey.
Therefore it is said that those who harbor lustful dispositions constitute one form of evil conduct.

Furthermore, when parents raise a child—conceiving, giving birth, and nurturing them until they reach adulthood—the toil and hardship involved are beyond description. Once the child has grown, fearing the depletion of family wealth, they crawl on their knees and elbows to seek a match through a go-between, expressing their feelings to bring about a marriage. If the partner is in a distant land, they pursue them regardless of the distance or the hardship endured, their minds fixed solely on lust while neglecting their own aged parents. Having obtained a wife, they cherish her as a treasure, seeking private pleasure and loathing the sight of their parents. Believing in her seductive words, they may even cause strife and litigation, failing to consider from whom they themselves were born or the immeasurable kindness of their solitary parents.
These are called the two evil dispositions.

Furthermore, there are those who, living in this world, undergo diligent toil and exhaustion to acquire wealth for themselves; they originally possess sincerity and faith, as well as a mind that reveres the Way and honors śramaṇas and brahmins; they perceive that the world is impermanent and regard giving as a source of merit.

After taking a wife, one’s emotions become deluded by lust and ignorance shrouds the mind; turning one's back on the True and heading toward the perverse is solely due to female form. If one possesses the intention to practice giving, yet when wishing to speak, one calls out to female forms instead, severing pure conduct and becoming a petty person; failing to recognize the precepts of the Buddhist scriptures or the destination of karmic retribution, one will perversely pursue lustful desires and cast oneself into a snare, inevitably falling into the evil realms without ever reforming.

These are called the three evil dispositions. Furthermore, as a son, one does not merely contemplate the kindness of being nurtured; yet, in managing one’s livelihood and acquiring wealth, one does not do so to support one’s parents. Instead, one seeks out paths of debauchery far and wide, carrying precious goods to entice the wives of others. Or, one slaughters six-footed beasts to perform licentious sacrifices to spirits and deities. After drinking wine, singing, and dancing in such gatherings, they seek further opportunities to summon one another to fulfill their lewd desires. When they finally find a mate, their joy is beyond description; bound and fettered by lust, they lose all sense of discernment.

At that time, one perceives only this as pleasure, unaware of the foul stench of impurities or the agonizing suffering of hell; it is both laughable and terrifying, like a rabid dog that does not know its own error.
"These are called the four evil dispositions.
The Buddha said:
"If a man possesses these four evils, he will fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, one should carefully distance oneself from these dispositions to escape suffering."
Furthermore, listen to the evils of women.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Already driven by desire, One lets the mind run wild and cannot find peace.”
Practicing giving through unrighteous means—how can one be considered virtuous?
To act out of desire is to behave like a beast; by such desire, one brings calamity upon oneself.
Like a dung-worm in the midst of stench, one does not realize the difficulty of its dwelling place.
Like an insect in the darkness, Not knowing east from west,
Bound and attached to sensual desire— This "Treatise on the Insect" also censures this.
Since lust prevents one from seeing the Path, Day and night it plants the roots of evil.
In this present age, lords and ministers are in chaos; those above and below are mired in confusion.
The royal law is disordered, and the True Dharma is obstructed by delusion.
Farmers abandon their regular labors, while merchants amass heaps of precious goods.
In this present life one enters further prisons; after death, one enters Mount Tai.
One must undergo a hundred kinds of poison, its agony difficult to endure.
Molten copper is poured into one’s mouth, and mountains press together to crush one’s body.
These groups number in the hundreds, and it would be difficult to describe them one by one.
They constantly dwell in the three evil realms, revolving like the wheels of a cart;
even when a Buddha appears in the world at such times, they do not get to hear his teaching.
Women are the most evil; it is difficult to form a causal connection with them.
Bound by the fetters of affection and love, they lead people into the gates of transgression.
What is so good about women?
This is but a bag of excrement and urine; why do you not examine it with clear vision? For what reason are you so deranged and wild?
Within, it is utterly foul and filthy, yet on the outside you adorn its appearance.
A home harboring venomous scorpions is as terrible as a serpent with a dragon.
It is like a brocade sheath for a spear, or fine gauze covering a sharp blade;
the fool beholds only its exterior and toys with it to his own ruin.
The wise man perceives this and casts it aside; the deluded person brings about death and injury.
Sensual desire is likewise so: it is like embracing a blade to bring about one's own ruin.
Upon seeing the new, one immediately grows weary of the old; that which is enjoyed is impermanent.
Speech is like being severed by a sword or axe; laughter is like thorns and brambles.
Within they harbor foul and poisonous filth, yet they adorn the exterior with flowers and incense;
the deluded person craves its flavor, failing to consider the calamity to come.
It is like a venomous poison mixed with ambrosial nectar.
Wherever it goes, nothing remains unsmashed; those who drink it all fall prostrate and stiff.
It is like fire meeting kindling, or grass and trees struck by heavy frost.
To observe only the outward appearance without reckoning the inner substance is the height of lack of discernment.
The poison of women is even more severe than this; it manifests its injury through the body.
To sever desire in order to seek the Way, one must recognize that lustful passion exists;
its form is very easy to perceive, yet the minds of the deluded do not sever it.
A net is spread across the four directions, yet one’s distance from the Way is but a hair’s breadth.
Man is originally of pure nature, like a fish dwelling in the deep abyss;
only the wise awaken to this themselves, for once caught in the net, one cannot return.
The net of desire is even more extensive than this; its bonds are even firmer than desire.
One might cast oneself into thorns and yet manage to escape one's body;
it is like a hungry monkey who, upon seeing ripe and sweet fruit, gazes longingly at it.
Single-mindedly casting themselves into sensual desires, these people fall into ruin in a hundred ways.
Like fish swallowing the hook or moths entering the flame,
the foolish see only joy and do not consider the calamity they will suffer hereafter.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, King Udayana was filled with joy. He immediately prostrated himself, touching his head to the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Truly, since birth I have never heard of such evil in women. Men fall into transgression by following their rebellious and chaotic impulses; it is only because they do not realize this that they do not restrain their minds."
"From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I shall repent of my transgressions; I take refuge in the Triple Gem and dare not commit such offenses again.
Having paid homage to the Buddha, he departed with joy.
Thus ends the *Sūtra on King Udayana* spoken by the Buddha.
